units.translation: The oar-blade, then, and the course of the linen-sewn ship –– of the spear
I think, then, that they did not even attack the gates
Neither a great one nor, then, any of the young ones
May I neither be a sacker of cities nor, then, myself captured by others, see my life
Neither among goddesses seen by gods, nor, then, resembling mortal forms
Just as, then, with murder-dripping fortune the mind rages
Just as, then, his father perished
since the gods | the seat having been taken

Since this particle and the grammarians' observations about it have been discussed in Thes. vol. 5 p. 1055-1059, here it will be enough to note that the Attic poets used two forms, as the meter required, ἕνεκα [because] and οὕνεκα [because], while in Attic prose only ἕνεκα [because] was used, and no Attic author used the Ionic εἵνεκα [because], which scribes often introduced into the tragedians and Aristophanes in place of οὕνεκα [because], except Sophocles, in whom ἕνεκα [because] and εἵνεκα [because] are never read, but always οὕνεκα [because], and Aeschylus, in whom ἕνεκα [because] is read once, Ag. 800, and εἵνεκα [because] was introduced only once in place of οὕνεκα [because], Suppl. 188. Moreover, οὕνεκα [because] is contracted from οὗ ἕνεκα [for which reason], just as ὁθούνεκα [because] (which Aeschylus used once for ὅτι [that] Pr. 330 ζηλῶ σ᾽ ὁθούνεκ᾽ ἐκτὸς ἀἰτίας κυρεῖς [I envy you because you are free from blame]) arose from ὅτου ἕνεκα [for which reason], but by a certain misuse it came about that οὕνεκα [because] was also said for simple ἕνεκα [because] and οὕνεκα [because] was not only a conjunction meaning the same as ὅτι [that, because], but also a preposition meaning 'because of'. There are few examples in later inscriptions in which εἵνεκα, εἵνεκεν [because] and ἕνεκεν [because] are found, which Wecklein enumerated in his Curis epigraphicis p. 39, from which it cannot be concluded that the ancient Attic writers preferred to use Ionic εἵνεκα [because] rather than say οὕνεκα [because].
I envy you because you are free from blame
because of, preposition governing the genitive, either before or after it
Thus Heath for οὖν ἐκληρώθη [then was allotted]
for which much toil and much sea was plowed by the spear
